name: Simple plano-convex lens
kb: Ground and polished spherical single surface
note: The kernel is that a single spherical surface converges parallel light to a point. Aberrations are severe; useful only for low magnification.

name: Doublet achromatic lens
kb: Crown and flint glass cemented together to correct chromatic aberration
note: Red and blue light have different refractive indices; flint glass bends them oppositely. A concave flint inside a convex crown cancels the dispersion while keeping convergence. Cemented joint must be optically contacted.

name: Triplet apochromatic lens
kb: Three-glass combination corrects to secondary spectrum
note: Flint-crown-flint sandwich with carefully chosen thicknesses eliminates both primary and secondary chromatic aberration. Air gaps between elements are essential; spacing is critical.

name: Petzval portrait lens
kb: Rear convergent group and front achromat for high aperture
note: The kernel is that a convergent group behind the aperture stop naturally focuses field curvature to a curved surface, which is acceptable for portrait work where central sharpness matters. f/3.5 was revolutionary for 1840s photography.

name: Cooke triplet photographic lens
kb: Symmetrical three-element design for uniform field correction
note: Symmetry means left and right aberrations cancel; the central meniscus acts as field flattener. Astigmatism and coma are small across a wide field. This design persisted unchanged into the 1970s.

name: Tessar compound photographic lens
kb: Four-element design with cemented doublet
note: The rear doublet is cemented; front elements air-spaced. Tessar corrects all primary aberrations (spherical, coma, astigmatism, field curvature) and controls distortion. f/4.5 was standard for hand cameras 1902-1950.

name: Telephoto lens principle
kb: Converging front, diverging rear, makes focal length exceed physical length
note: The interval between front and rear elements is shorter than focal length; magnification and physical compactness are the point. Rear element separation tunes back working distance.

name: Wide angle photographic lens
kb: Reversed Petzval or symmetrical design, focal length shorter than image diagonal
note: Large field angle means massive distortion if not corrected. Symmetrical designs minimize distortion at the cost of vignetting. Focal length/image diagonal ratio defines angle of view.

name: Telescope primary mirror parabolic
kb: Parabolic surface focuses parallel light to point; thin speculum metal or silvered glass
note: The parabola corrects spherical aberration; a sphere would have offaxis focus. Speculums corrode; silvered glass requires maintenance every few years. Precision to 0.1 wavelength required for good focus.

name: Cassegrain reflector telescope
kb: Secondary convex mirror bounces light back through hole in primary
note: Effective focal length can be very large; physical tube is short and stiff. Secondary blockage costs light; useful for high magnification and spectroscopy. Cassegrain and Gregorian differ in secondary curvature (convex vs concave).

name: Newtonian reflector telescope
kb: Flat mirror at 45 degrees directs focal point to side of tube
note: Simple and cheap; no secondary mirror obstruction. Off-axis aberrations manageable up to f/4. The flat (Newtonian diagonal) must be very small (5-15% blockage) and precisely angled.

name: Schmidt corrector plate
kb: Aspheric glass plate corrects spherical mirror aberrations; wide field possible
note: A spherical mirror has severe offaxis aberrations. A thin aspheric plate near the center of curvature corrects all of them. Requires precision figuring to waves; small deviations ruin image.

name: Prism: Amici roof prism
kb: Roof-shaped prism erects image and folds light path for compact binoculars
note: The roof angle must be precisely 90 degrees; any error causes the two roof faces to produce a split image. Coating the roof faces was later improvement.

name: Prism: Porro prism binocular
kb: Two 45-90-45 prisms erect image and separate exit pupils for eye relief
note: Porro gives longer eyepiece separation than roof; better for binoculars where one prism arm doubles as the barrel. Internal reflections must not degrade contrast.

name: Beam splitter dichroic mirror
kb: Partial reflector divides light into two paths; angle selects wavelength with coatings
note: Evaporated metal films or dielectric coatings create partial reflectors. Dichroic effect (color-dependent reflection) requires interference; multilayer coatings achieve sharp wavelength separation.

name: Polariser: Nicol prism calcite
kb: Birefringent calcite transmits one polarisation state, rejects other
note: Natural birefringence of calcite; extraordinary ray and ordinary ray have different refractive indices. Carving and cementing a prism at the Brewster angle transmits one, reflects the other internally.

name: Wave plate phase retarder
kb: Anisotropic crystal retards one polarisation by fraction of wavelength
note: Quarter wave plate shifts phase by 90 degrees; half wave by 180. Thickness controls retardation. Mica easily cleaves to controlled thickness; later crystals like quartz are more stable.

name: Interference filter coated
kb: Multilayer dielectric coatings create bandpass filter by coherent reflection
note: Alternating high and low index layers create destructive interference outside the pass band. Extremely narrow passbands possible; sharp edges. Requires vacuum evaporation and strict thickness control.

name: Antireflection coating single wavelength
kb: Quarter-wave coating reduces reflection from 4% to <0.1% at one wavelength
note: A single quarter-wave layer of the right index nearly halves losses at design wavelength; this doubled the effective aperture of telescopes and microscopes. Multicoatings extend bandwidth.

name: Reticle: crosshair or graticule
kb: Fine lines or dots etched or photographed onto glass plate
note: Etching with diamond point or photographic reduction defines the graticule. Registration of crosshairs to optical axis is the precision step.

name: Eyepiece: Huygens
kb: Two plano-convex lenses separated by their focal lengths
note: Lens separation equals the sum of focal lengths; real image forms between elements. Long eye relief and wide field for low powers; chromatic aberration high.

name: Eyepiece: Kellner
kb: Plano-convex field lens and achromatic eyelens
note: Achromatic eyelens corrects the Huygens problem; large field of view; good eye relief. Became standard for 19th-century microscopes.

name: Eyepiece: Ramsden
kb: Two identical plano-convex lenses cemented or close-spaced
note: Real image forms between lenses; reticle can be placed there. Simpler than Kellner and Huygens. Used for surveying instruments where a graticule is essential.

name: Eyepiece: Orthoscopic
kb: Triplet eyelens with wide flat field and high magnification
note: All aberrations well corrected; distortion nearly absent. Best planetary observation eyepiece until the Erfle; good for telescopes of any focal ratio.

name: Eyepiece: Erfle wide field
kb: Five-element wide field eyepiece with 60-68 degree angle of view
note: The kernel: five elements can be tuned to flatten field and correct all aberrations across a wide angle. Previous 3-4 element designs limited to 50 degrees.

name: Condenser: sub-stage aperture control
kb: Converging lens below the sample focuses illumination and houses iris diaphragm
note: Iris diaphragm controls numerical aperture of illumination; matching it to objective NA maximizes contrast and depth of field. Substage height adjustment focuses the light.

name: Immersion objective: oil lens
kb: Objective designed to work through oil between lens and coverslip; refractive index matched
note: Oil (n=1.52) matches glass closely; light bent less at air-glass interface, allowing higher NA. Allows numerical apertures above 1.0, finer resolution. Standard for 1000x magnification.

name: Phase contrast objective and annuli
kb: Annular source and phase plate convert amplitude variations to visible contrast
note: Transparent samples have tiny amplitude differences that the eye cannot detect; phase differences are huge but invisible. Phase plate retards diffracted light; interference makes phases visible. Revolutionary for biology.

name: Dark field condenser: oblique illumination
kb: Light cone with large angle misses objective; only scattered light enters
note: Unstained samples are nearly invisible in brightfield because they scatter little and absorb little. Dark field cuts direct light; scattered light from particles appears bright on black background.

name: Ultramicroscope: dark field with slit lamp
kb: Intense line source illuminates specimen at high angle; Tyndall scattering visible
note: Colloid particles smaller than visible wavelength scatter light; ultramicroscope can detect particles 10-100 nm, below direct visibility limit. Used to verify kinetic theory of matter.

name: Microtome: sliding blade
kb: Blade slides past specimen; spring controls thickness; produces thin sections
note: Tissue freezes on stage; blade slides at angle; spring deflection determines slice thickness. 50-200 micron sections for hand microscopy.

name: Microtome: rotary feed
kb: Rotating handle advances specimen by screw; produces ribbons of thin serial sections
note: Screw advance per rotation is fixed and precise; blade remains stationary; hundreds of consecutive micron-thick sections from one specimen. Required for neuroanatomy.

name: Electron microscope: column and lens assembly
kb: Vacuum tube with high voltage, electromagnetic lenses focus electron beam
note: Electrons have wavelength 1000x smaller than visible light; 2000x higher resolution. Requires high vacuum, high voltage (50-100 kV), and magnetic lenses. Sample preparation and observation technique are complex.

name: Electron source: heated cathode
kb: Tungsten filament heated to 2700K; thermionic emission produces electron beam
note: Filament life determined by evaporation rate; higher temperature gives more current but shorter life. Wehnelt cap focuses emission. Tungsten chosen for high melting point and low evaporation.

name: Spectrograph: prism camera
kb: Prism disperses light; objective focuses spectrum onto photographic plate
note: Photography captures the spectrum without eye; much fainter lines visible. Comparison spectra on same plate enable precise wavelength measurement.

name: Spectrograph: grating camera
kb: Diffraction grating disperses light; objective focuses higher orders onto plate
note: Grating gives linear wavelength scale and multiple orders; more light concentrated. Requires grating of very high quality; defects are invisible to eye but ruin spectrum.

name: Diffraction grating: ruled reflective
kb: Thousands of parallel grooves per mm, ruled with precision screw and diamond
note: The kernel: fine pitch (20,000-50,000 lines/inch) requires a master screw with error < 0.1 micron over its full length. Groove uniformity is critical; defects scatter light.

name: Ruling engine: precision screw diamond
kb: Master screw with diamond point advances across glass or metal; grooves separated by wavelength precision
note: The most demanding instrument before 1950. Screw must advance uniformly against spring loading; spindle runout < 0.5 micron over 200 mm stroke. Most sophisticated mechanical device of its era.

name: Interferometer: Michelson
kb: Beam splitter divides light; mirrors reflect; recombined beams interfere
note: Adjustment is finicky; mirror angle must be within microradians. Fringe visibility depends on path difference being small. Used to measure length by counting fringes as mirror moves.

name: Interferometer: Fabry-Pérot etalon
kb: Two parallel silvered surfaces; light bounces many times; sharp resonance peaks
note: Multiple reflections enhance sharpness; useful for spectral lines separated by nanometers. Parallelism and surface flatness required to better than 0.1 wavelength.

name: Mass spectrograph: deflection
kb: Ions accelerated and deflected by magnetic field; detection plate measures trajectories
note: Radius of curvature proportional to mass; spot positions give isotope masses and abundances. Requires high vacuum, stable voltage, and precise ion source.

name: Cyclotron accelerator: magnet and RF coil
kb: Magnetic field bends particles in spiral; RF accelerates between gaps
note: Synchronism between particle orbit period and RF frequency is automatic; frequency stays constant as particle spirals outward and gains energy. Enables 10-20 MeV beam, impossible with accelerators.

name: Van de Graaff static generator
kb: Moving belt transfers charge to dome; voltage accumulates; sparks at high voltage
note: Belt isolation makes voltage independent of corona losses; millions of volts achievable. Originally thought impractical; elegant principle that charges accumulate without external energy beyond motor to drive belt.

name: Cloud chamber: Wilson expansion chamber
kb: Sudden expansion cools air to supersaturation; charged particles trigger condensation trails
note: The kernel: ions seed condensation; alcohol vapor becomes cloud along particle tracks. Photographs record tracks: alpha particles thick and straight, beta particles thin and curved, gamma rays occasional electron recoils.

name: Photographic emulsion detector
kb: Silver halide grains record particle tracks at nanometer resolution
note: Emulsion provides permanent record and extreme position resolution (< 1 micron). Quantitative analysis requires careful grain counting and calibration against known energies.

name: X-ray diffraction camera: Bragg geometry
kb: X-rays diffract from crystal planes; angles and intensities reveal atomic structure
note: Bragg angle = arcsin(wavelength / 2d); both angle and intensity must be measured. Requires collimated X-rays and precision rotation stage.

name: Electron diffraction camera: LEED
kb: Electrons diffract from crystal planes; low energy gives surface sensitivity
note: Electron wavelength < 1 Angstrom; very small diffraction angles. Phosphor screen detects diffraction pattern. Low-energy electrons (50-500 eV) scatter strongly from top layers.

name: Ultracentrifuge: high-speed rotor
kb: Rotor spins at 100,000 rpm; centrifugal field separates molecules by size
note: Rotor imbalance is catastrophic; dynamic balancing to < 1 gram-cm required. Vacuum jacket reduces drag and heating.

name: pH meter: glass electrode potentiometer
kb: Glass electrode voltage responds to hydrogen ion concentration; amplifier measures millivolts
note: Glass electrode potential is logarithmic in [H+]; high impedance requires vacuum tube amplifier. Slope and zero-point calibration against known buffers essential.

name: Oscilloscope: cathode ray tube display
kb: Electron beam deflected by electric or magnetic fields; strikes phosphor screen
note: Deflection sensitivity and time-base linearity are critical. Phosphor persistence determines trace brightness and flicker. High voltage supply must be stable.

name: Strain gauge: bonded resistance wire
kb: Wire resistance changes with strain; stretched wire has higher resistance
note: Temperature compensation via dummy gauge. Bridge circuit nulls initial resistance; strain produces bridge imbalance. Gauge factor (delta-R/R per unit strain) is material-dependent and reproducible.

name: Strain gauge bridge amplifier
kb: Wheatstone bridge with strain gauge and vacuum tube amplifier measures tiny resistance changes
note: Bridge balance point shifts with strain; amplified output is linear over useful range. Temperature drift in gauges and electronics is a constant problem.

name: Wind tunnel: subsonic test section
kb: Contoured duct delivers uniform flow; model attached; forces measured by balance
note: Boundary layer thickness and pressure gradient are critical to realistic results. Model blockage ratio must be < 5 percent. Inlet contraction and honeycomb reduce turbulence.

name: Shock tube: driven and dump sections
kb: Rupture diaphragm between high and low pressure gas; shock wave propagates
note: Temperature behind shock is predictable from gas properties and compression ratio; brief duration allows measurement at extreme conditions. Diaphragm timing is precise.

name: Towing tank: model boat resistance measurement
kb: Long water channel; model on carriage; drag measured against water balance
note: Model-to-full-scale scaling requires Reynolds number matching; separate friction and pressure drag requires careful measurement of local pressure.

name: Vibration table: shaker with electromagnet
kb: Armature driven by AC field; table oscillates at mains frequency; amplitude controlled
note: Mechanical resonances of specimen must be understood; forced excitation can produce nonlinear effects. Force and displacement must both be measured.

name: Fatigue test machine: rotating bending
kb: Sample in rotating fixture; stress oscillates sinusoidally; failure recorded vs cycle count
note: Specimen rotates through constant bending moment; every point sees same stress cycle. Failure always begins at stress concentration; S-N curve (stress vs cycle count) defines fatigue limit.

name: Creep furnace: constant load at high temperature
kb: Specimen held at fixed stress and temperature; elongation measured vs time
note: Creep rate accelerates with time; elongation logarithmic or power-law in time. Material structure changes under stress; microstructure analysis explains rate.

name: High pressure cell: diamond anvil or autoclave
kb: Hydraulic or screw press confines sample; pressure measured by pressure gauge
note: Diamond anvil for optics; hardened steel for liquids. Seal design and pressure measurement calibration are critical.

name: Cryostat: dewar flask double-walled
kb: Vacuum between walls; liquid nitrogen or helium maintains cryogenic temperature
note: Vacuum insulation much better than solid foam (which didn't exist); radiation baffle reduces heat transfer. Silver coating reflects infrared.

name: Joule-Thomson expansion valve
kb: Gas expands through throttle; cooling is proportional to enthalpy drop
note: Cooling power depends on entering pressure and temperature; for most gases, Joule-Thomson coefficient is positive (cooling). Throttle design (capillary or sintered restriction) controls expansion.

name: Linde cycle: expansion engine and recuperator
kb: Compressed gas cools against expanding outflow; cascade stages liquefy air
note: Each stage drops temperature; tail gas cools incoming gas. Requires pure, dry air (CO2 and water freeze out). Liquefaction rate 1-10 liters/hour.

name: Claude cycle: air liquefaction with work extraction
kb: Expander cools more efficiently than Joule-Thomson; some gas expands to do work
note: Expander is efficiency gain: gas does external work while cooling. Allows higher input temperature before liquefaction. Industrial version dominates after 1920.

name: Adiabatic demagnetization apparatus
kb: Magnetic field aligns spins; adiabatic removal of field allows spins to disorder, cooling
note: Cooling power limited by entropy of spin system; achieves 0.01 K from starting 1 K. Requires precision heat switches and careful thermometry.

name: Measuring chain: steel links
kb: 66 feet (20 m) of steel links; handles at ends; numbered every 10 links
note: Standardization of link length was critical; earlier chains varied between regions. Stretch under tension; calibration against standard required.

name: Steel measuring tape: wound on reel
kb: 100-300 feet steel tape; tension handle and brake; gradient mark for slope distance
note: Tape sags under its own weight; standard tension (100 lbs) specified in manuals. Thermal expansion significant for steel; correction tables provided.

name: Spirit level: bubble in tube
kb: Curved tube 90% filled with alcohol; bubble indicates deviation from horizontal
note: Curvature of tube determines sensitivity; tighter curve = smaller bubble movement for given tilt. Sensitivity 1 minute of arc typical.

name: Theodolite: angle measurement
kb: Telescope with two perpendicular rotating circles; horizontal and vertical angles
note: Circles divided 360 degrees with minute precision; verniers read to 10 seconds. Optics give magnification; telescope focuses on distant point.

name: Tacheometer: distance and elevation measurement
kb: Theodolite with special stadia reticle; staff reading gives distance directly
note: Stadia interval subtends known angle; staff distance = staff reading / tangent of angle. Avoids chain for rough work; less accurate but much faster.

name: Plane table: graphical surveying
kb: Board on tripod; graphite paper and straightedge; draw map directly in field
note: Immediate feedback on map; errors caught in field. Slope corrections and magnetic declination must be handled separately. Useful for small-area mapping.

name: Alidade: sight ruler for plane table
kb: Ruler with telescopic sights; sets direction on map from observation point
note: Telescope provides magnification and collimation; eyepiece must be designed to give clear view of distant point while keeping edge of ruler in sight.

name: Triangulation: station marker
kb: Stable tripod with fixed marks for theodolite centering
note: Centering error contributes to position error; forced centering (rotating theodolite over fixed point) necessary for high precision.

name: Baseline measurement: apparatus and calibration
kb: Known length baseline; correction for slope, temperature, tension; used as reference for triangulation
note: Baseline length accuracy sets precision of entire survey; errors in baseline are magnified by triangulation. Careful temperature and tension control during measurement.

name: Geodetic survey apparatus complete
kb: Network of triangulation points; height determined by precise levelling
note: National survey requires coordination of many teams over years. Control points must be stable; pillar stability checked periodically.

name: Precise levelling: rod and staff
kb: Calibrated rod with mm graduations; telescope focuses on graticule; difference of sights gives height difference
note: Backsight and foresight must balance to third decimal place; systematic errors (refraction, curvature) cancel only if distances equal. Levelling bench marks established every km.

name: Gravimeter: spring balance portable
kb: Mass hangs on calibrated spring; period or deflection indicates local gravity
note: Gravity variation 0.3 percent across Earth; instrument detects 0.01 percent. Thermal compensation by bimetallic strips essential.

name: Magnetometer: sensitive compass
kb: Magnetic needle suspended by fine quartz fiber; deflection angle measures field
note: Temperature and vibration affect needle; declination charts required for navigation. Magnetic latitude determines angle of dip.

name: Sextant: arc and optical system
kb: Moving mirror superimposes sun or star images; arc angle gives latitude or distance
note: Optical path via fixed and moving mirrors allows 60 degree field in 120 degree arc. Reading to 0.1 arcminute requires careful eyepiece and vernier.

name: Artificial horizon: bubble level
kb: Small spirit level defines horizontal reference when sea horizon is not visible
note: Bubble much more visible than faint horizon at twilight; altitude star not twice-the-bubble correction because half the motion needed.

name: Marine chronometer: spring balance compensation
kb: Balance spring oscillator; bimetallic compensation maintains frequency at sea temperature variation
note: Chronometer rate (gain/loss per day) must be < 1 second; observed rate used to correct while at sea. Ship's motion and temperature gradients are constant challenges.

name: Chronometer rate observation
kb: Lunar distance or lunar occultation gives time; chronometer rate determined
note: Greenwich time determined independently; comparison over several days averages out daily variations.

name: Sounding machine: lead line and marks
kb: Weighted rope marked every fathom; bottom sample in cavity of lead
note: Sample of bottom (sand, mud, shells) helps identify location when fog prevents sight navigation. Deep sea (> 300 fathoms) requires stronger line.

name: Echo sounder: acoustic depth finder
kb: Spark or transducer emits sound pulse; reflected echo arrives after time proportional to depth
note: Sound speed in water 1500 m/s; modern instruments use frequency sweep. Early spark sounders were intermittent; later continuous recordings possible.

name: Gyrocompass: spinning rotor
kb: Rotor spins at high speed; gravity precession aligns axis with meridian
note: North-seeking property is automatic once spinning; no magnetic compass needed. Gyroscopic inertia suppresses ship's motion effects.

name: Gyro horizon: attitude indicator
kb: Gyroscope spin axis maintains reference; precession from aircraft maneuvers indicated on dial
note: Gyroscopic inertia holds attitude; erection mechanism cancels slow drift. Precession rate ~ mass imbalance * gravity.

name: Radio direction finder: loop antenna
kb: Loop antenna orientation for minimum signal indicates bearing to transmitter
note: Dipole pattern of loop gives sharp null; bearing is direction of null. 180-degree ambiguity resolved by sense antenna or manual observation.

name: Aerial camera: gyro-stabilized mount
kb: Camera mounted on gyroscopic platform; vibration isolation allows sharp photos from aircraft
note: Focal length and shutter speed set by altitude and aircraft speed; sidelap and endlap of frames ensures stereoscopic overlap.

name: Photogrammetry: stereoscope and comparator
kb: Pair of aerial photos viewed stereoscopically; parallax gives elevation; comparator measures precise positions
note: Optical axis separation and focal length known from calibration; parallax difference = height difference. Systematic errors from camera tilt must be corrected.

name: Photometer: visual brightness comparison
kb: Light source compared to standard candle; intensity by distance inverse-square law
note: Standard candle defined (1 candela); distance squared from unknown source matched to known distance from standard.

name: Bolometer: blackened platinum resistance
kb: Blackened metal foil heated by infrared; resistance change measured
note: Time constant must be < 0.1 second to follow modulated light; thermal mass vs sensitivity tradeoff.

name: Photocell: vacuum photoelectric
kb: Photon ejects electron from cathode; current proportional to light intensity
note: Quantum efficiency 5-10 percent; spectral response depends on cathode material. Cathode sensitivity to residual gas vapor is problem.

name: Photomultiplier: secondary emission cascade
kb: Initial photocurrent amplified by secondary emission from dynode chain
note: Gain 10^6 typical; enables detection of single photons. Dark current (thermioni emission) limits low-light sensitivity; cooling essential.

name: Spectral radiometer: grating and photocells
kb: Spectrum dispersed by grating; many photocells measure intensity at different wavelengths
note: Array of detectors measures entire spectrum; much faster than scanning monochromator. Calibration against blackbody standard essential.

name: Electroscope: gold leaf detector
kb: Gold leaf suspended from high-potential conductor; repulsion angle indicates charge
note: Leaf must be thin and light; damped oscillation with critical damping optimal. Used to detect radioactivity by ionisation of air.

name: Ionisation chamber: gas filled detector
kb: Gas ionised by radiation; ions collected by electric field; current measured
note: Signal proportional to energy; used to measure radiation intensity. Electrode spacing and voltage fixed; gas filling critical.

name: Geiger-Müller counter: proportional region
kb: Gas avalanche multiplication in cylindrical electrode; each ion produces 10^6 electrons
note: Pulse output independent of input energy (above threshold); excellent counting efficiency. Dead time 100-300 microseconds limits count rate.

name: Scintillation detector: crystal and photomultiplier
kb: Radiation hits crystal; fluorescence photons counted by photomultiplier
note: Energy resolution better than Geiger counter; pulse height gives particle energy. Decay time of scintillation limits count rate (1000 cps typical).

name: Travelling microscope for length measurement
kb: Microscope mounted on precision screw; stage position read to 0.01 mm
note: Magnification gives visual precision on micrometer screw. Kernel is matching optical resolution to mechanical precision of the screw.

name: Optical comparator: magnified shadow projection
kb: Light source projects magnified shadow of part onto screen with graticule
note: Magnification 10x-100x; edge sharpness depends on light source coherence. Faster than microscope for many parts; no contact with surface.

name: Analytical balance: equal arm
kb: Knife-edge pivot; pans on either side; rider weight determines mass
note: Sensitivity depends on balance arm length and pivot sharpness. Rider on beam allows fractional weights.

name: Torsion balance: vertical fiber suspension
kb: Mass suspended on quartz fiber; torsion angle measured by mirror deflection
note: No knife edge; fiber can twist billions of times. Used to measure gravitational constant and test inverseness of gravitational law.

name: Microbalance: quartz oscillator frequency shift
kb: Thin quartz disk vibrates at natural frequency; mass deposited on surface shifts frequency
note: Sensitivity nanogram range; frequency stable to 0.01 Hz. Used for film thickness measurement and chemical detection.

name: Thermocouple: junction EMF measurement
kb: Two dissimilar metals joined; temperature difference produces EMF proportional to delta-T
note: Seebeck coefficient and reference junction temperature define sensitivity. High-temperature range extends to 1600 C with platinum-platinum/rhodium.

name: Resistance thermometer: platinum RTD
kb: Platinum wire resistance increases linearly with temperature; measured by bridge circuit
note: Accuracy better than thermocouple; slow response. Industrial platinum RTDs have 0.1 C accuracy. Insulation resistance can limit precision.

name: Gas thermometry: absolute temperature scale
kb: Constant-volume or constant-pressure gas thermometer; defines absolute zero and Kelvin scale
note: Kernel is that gas pressure or volume change is linear with absolute temperature. Primary standard used to calibrate mercury and resistance thermometers. Requires careful control of gas amount.

name: Mercury barometer: column height
kb: Mercury column in evacuated tube; height indicates atmospheric pressure
note: Standard atmosphere = 760 mm Hg at 0 C and 45 degrees latitude. Correction for latitude, temperature, and mercury density variation required for precision.

name: Aneroid pressure gauge: evacuated bellows
kb: Evacuated metal capsule flexes with pressure; linkage amplifies motion to pointer
note: No liquid; portable and rugged. Accuracy 2-3 percent typical for barometers. Frequency response for recording dynamic pressure is much better than mercury column.

name: Bourdon tube pressure gauge
kb: Flattened curved tube straightens under pressure; deflection indicates gauge pressure
note: Works up to 1000 bar with steel tubes. Nonlinearity and hysteresis are issues; C-tube, spiral, and helical forms trade span for linearity.

name: McLeod gauge: compression manometer
kb: Gas trapped in graduated tube and compressed against mercury column; pressure from height drop
note: Measures 1 to 1e-4 torr. Requires careful construction and leveling. Provides absolute calibration for other gauges.

name: Quartz resonator: piezoelectric oscillator
kb: Quartz crystal cut and polished; piezoelectric effect creates oscillation at resonant frequency
note: Frequency stability better than 1 part per million per year. Replaced tuning forks for precise timekeeping. Frequency depends on crystal cut and temperature.

name: Orifice plate: differential pressure flow measurement
kb: Restricted opening in pipe; pressure drop upstream and downstream is proportional to flow rate squared
note: Cheap and simple; but discharge coefficient depends on Reynolds number and geometry. Pressure recovery poor.

name: Venturi tube: smooth convergent-divergent flow
kb: Smooth contraction and expansion; pressure drop in throat measures flow rate
note: Better pressure recovery than orifice; more stable discharge coefficient. Smooth internal surface essential for accuracy.

name: Pitot tube: total and static pressure difference
kb: Stagnation pressure at nose minus static pressure gives dynamic pressure = 0.5 rho v^2
note: Yields velocity directly from pressure difference. Sensitive to flow angularity; probe design critical for accuracy in turbulent flow.

name: Balance spring: spiral hairspring
kb: Thin spiral steel spring driving balance wheel; frequency defines watch rate
note: Isochronism (period independent of amplitude) requires specific curve shape. Compensation for thermal expansion uses bimetallic rim. Precision chronometer rates to seconds per week.

name: Tuning fork: acoustic resonator
kb: Two prongs vibrate in opposition; frequency determined by mass and stiffness
note: Frequency stable to 0.1 percent; frequencies 100 Hz to 1000 Hz common. Used as timekeeping standard before quartz.
